uses.quote: Generate ideas - but not generate assessed work: AI can be used to assist you in generating ideas
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of generative AI in assessments

uses.quote: Clarification: using AI to clarify doubts, seek explanations, or understand complex vocabulary or sentence structures, but not as a substitute for deeper analysis and comprehension when producing assessed work.
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of generative AI in assessments

uses.quote: Further reading and research: seeking suggestions for additional resources or references related to the topic.
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of generative AI in assessments

uses.quote: Requesting direct answers or responses: asking generative AI your assessment questions or titles, and then using the generated response in assessed work without approval or attribution.
uses.anchor: Examples of poor and/or unacceptable use of generative AI in assessments

uses.quote: Submitting chunks of unedited text generated by AI: submitting academic work that is partly or entirely generated using AI, without any personal review, understanding, or modification, will be deemed false authorship.
uses.anchor: Examples of poor and/or unacceptable use of generative AI in assessments

uses.quote: Uncritical acceptance: accepting suggestions without critical evaluation, careful review, or consideration of accuracy, context or appropriateness will likely not only lead to a case of misconduct but also increase your chances of receiving a low grade.
uses.anchor: Examples of poor and/or unacceptable use of generative AI in assessments

uses.quote: some assessments will be held under closed exam conditions, where you will not be able to use any of the tools or services discussed.
uses.anchor: Warnings

uses.quote: over reliance on machine translation to the extent that it diminishes your active involvement and understanding, and results in false authorship, is strictly prohibited.
uses.anchor: Translation tools or services (human or digital)

uses.quote: If used in an appropriate way, and if permitted in your assignments, the use of online LEAs is not considered academic misconduct and can be beneficial during degree programme.
uses.anchor: Language-enhancement applications and proofreading services

uses.quote: Using automated paraphrasing tools, for example, can result in work of false authorship being submitted (as well as often poor paraphrasing!) and means you are not applying the skills that you are here to learn.
uses.anchor: Language-enhancement applications and proofreading services

uses.quote: AI can be used to assist you in generating ideas, but again, this should not be a shortcut for critical thinking, deeper analysis and academic writing, all of which should be your own and you should be able to explain if asked.
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of generative AI in assessments

uses.quote: Learning enhancement: utilising generative AI to deepen understanding, explore complex concepts, and reinforce learning in the preparation stages of assessments.
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of generative AI in assessments

uses.quote: for many of your assessments (and unless otherwise stated), there will be a strict expectation that any use of generative AI in the production of work you submit will adhere to University policy regarding false authorship.
uses.anchor: Generative artificial intelligence (AI)

uses.quote: As a dictionary: translating a word, collocation or phrasal level when writing and reading text.
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of translation services or tools in assessments

uses.quote: As a language learning aid: to support language learning and improve proficiency by comparing translations with the original text, identifying vocabulary, checking pronunciation, and grasping grammatical structures.
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of translation services or tools in assessments

uses.quote: Translating work into the language of assessment: submitting academic work that is entirely generated using machine translation or a human translator, without any personal review, understanding, or modification.
uses.anchor: Examples of poor and/or unacceptable use of translation services or tools in assessments

uses.quote: Please also note that some assessments will prohibit translation entirely, and/or you will be unable to access translation tools (such as in closed exams or oral assessments).
uses.anchor: Translation tools or services (human or digital)

uses.quote: Grammar and language improvement: utilising LEAs to improve grammar, syntax, punctuation, and overall language structure to enhance the clarity and coherence of your academic writing.
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of LEAs in assessments

uses.quote: Excessive dependency: if your assessment submission has substitutions which appear to be that of a third party and not your own work, it will be deemed false authorship.
uses.anchor: Examples of poor and/or unacceptable use of LEAs in assessments

uses.quote: Vocabulary enrichment: using LEAs in a considered way to expand and enrich your vocabulary, aiding in the selection of appropriate and precise words for academic expression.
uses.anchor: Examples of good and/or acceptable use of LEAs in assessments

decided_by.quote: As always, check your assessment briefs and guidelines carefully, and if you are not sure about acceptable use, ask your teacher or coordinator.
If you are not sure whether it is acceptable to use generative AI content tools, you should discuss this with your programme leaders, module leaders or supervisors as soon as possible.
This guidance applies to students on undergraduate and postgraduate taught courses and should be used in conjunction with the Policy on acceptable assistance in assessment.

records.quote: It is advisable to keep records of the work you have done and to save different copies of your work rather than overwriting the same file all the time.

consequence.quote: ‘False authorship’ refers to creating or modifying academic work, either fully or partially, using unauthorised or undisclosed help from people (eg family, proofreaders, essay mills) or technology (eg generative AI, software, machine translation) without approval or acknowledgment and to such an extent that you can no longer be considered the author of the work.
